transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-08-29
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Evan Park (Redwood AE), Priya Rao (Redwood SE), Liam O'Neal (Redwood Solutions), Daniel Ortega (Luminex Head of ML), Rina Zhang (Luminex SRE), Marco Silva (CTO), Asha Patel (Platform)

Summary (auto): quick technical review of dynamic prefix routing, cache key strategy, and tenant isolation. Focus: hit-rate targets, collision mitigation, fallback and routing policies, VPC/on-prem constraints and quantization tradeoffs. Agreed next steps: docs, bench run, security artifacts.

Topics: prefix key design; consistent hashing vs tenant sharding; dynamic routing by latency/cost; KV cache poisoning and safety; eviction strategies; hybrid on-prem + hosted routing; quantization effect on cache compatibility; batching and tail latency.

Transcript:
[00:00] Evan: okay, hey everyone thanks for joining, i'll kick us off. we're here to go over dynamic prefix routing and tenant safety, especially around hit rates and how you all want to treat shared cache versus per-tenant siloing.
[00:18] Daniel: yeah thanks evan, we appreciate it. quick context: we run an in-house inference mesh on prem for PII workloads, and then cloud for lower-sensitivity customer support stuff. today we wanted to validate a caching strategy that reduces tokens to our expensive rigs.
[00:30] Priya: great. can you share current numbers? what qps, typical prompt lengths, and current cache hit rate?
[00:38] Rina: sure, so our live is about 120 qps average, peaks to 420 during batch windows. avg prompt length is 88 tokens, but there's a big tail of 600+ token docs. our naive prefix cache hit rate right now is about 9-12% because we key on whole prompt fingerprints and that rarely matches.
[01:00] Evan: okay that's helpful, and are you doing any prefix normalization like stripping user names, timestamps?
[01:06] Marco: yes some. we run a preprocessor that masks email and phone numbers, and basic normalizations. but the problem is we have a ton of near-duplicate prompts with slight role/context differences.
[01:18] Priya: that is the common case. the general approach we recommend is a multi-tiered key scheme: short prefix signatures for conversational intents + longer hashed context for exact-match. that lets you hit on intent-level reuse without returning stale or wrong sensitive outputs.
[01:36] Daniel: intent-level reuse sounds risky — what if the prefix maps to a different tenant's policy? we can't leak policy or private templates across tenants.
[01:45] Priya: absolutely, tenant isolation is primary. there are a few patterns: 1) strict per-tenant namespace — every cache key includes tenant id, or 2) shared hotset with tenant-aware validation: cache is shared, but responses include metadata and a revalidation path that rejects if policy mismatch. each has tradeoffs for memory and hit rate.
[02:06] Rina: can you expand on metadata revalidation? sounds like extra round trips.
[02:12] Priya: yeah it's an extra check but lightweight. when a shared hotset is hit, the runtime returns a signature and metadata like model variant, quantization profile, and tenant policies used to generate. the caller validates compatibility — if mismatch, fallback to live inference. the extra cost is a few hundred microseconds but you retain higher hit-rate for common prompts.
[02:31] Evan: a concrete example — say tenant A and B both have similar onboarding prompts. with per-tenant keys you get no cross-tenant hit. with shared hotset plus tenant validation, you can reuse candidate tokens but guard against policy drift.
[02:44] Marco: ok but that's more complicated for us because our compliance team wants a hard boundary for certain data classes. any shared cache must be opt-in per tenant.
[02:53] Priya: that's fair — the platform supports tenant-level policies to mark a tenant as "siloed". for those, we do per-tenant key prefixes and encrypt keys at rest with tenant KMS keys when on-prem V P C.
[03:07] Daniel: quick Q on collisions — you mentioned consistent hashing earlier. how do you avoid prefix hash collisions causing wrong reuse?
[03:14] Priya: collision probability is low with 128-bit signatures, but the more pressing issue is functional collision — different prompts that semantically diverge but produce same compact key because we aggressively truncate. our mitigation is hierarchical keys: (intent_sig, short_context_sig, full_hash). routing prefers intent_sig hits but requires accompanying context match to reuse the cached kv. we also maintain a small LRU exact-match layer for high-confidence responses.
[03:42] [03:42] Liam: (background voice) also add anti-poisoning — we rate-limit writes for low-trust tenants or untrusted prompts to avoid cache pollution.
[03:48] Rina: when you say intent_sig, what algorithm? minhash, simhash, or transformer-based embedding cluster?
[03:55] Priya: we typically use a lightweight simhash on normalized token streams for intent-level identification — low CPU and stable. for teams that can afford the cost, we have optional embedding-cluster keys (cosine) which are more robust but add compute.
[04:10] Daniel: how does quantization affect cache compatibility? we have mixed model fleet — bf16 in cloud, int8 on prem, and quantized variants.
[04:18] Priya: good point — cache entries are tied to model profile: architecture, seq-len, and quantization profile. key metadata includes model fingerprint. runtime routing will only reuse cache entries when the serving model is compatible (e.g., same decoder logits semantics). otherwise fallback. in practice, int8/int4 changes token probabilities slightly, so we limit reuse across different quantization unless you accept a small degrade.
[04:41] Marco: degrade is a no-go for customer visible answers. what about running a validation set to quantify divergence?
[04:46] Priya: exactly what we recommend — run a small validation workload and compute n-gram diffs and downstream metric regressions. we'll include that in the benchmark run.
[04:56] Evan: back to routing — you asked about dynamic prefix routing. that's the idea of selecting to serve from local on-prem model vs routing to hosted inference based on latency SLO, cost budget, and cache availability.
[05:07] Asha: our network egress to hosted is limited and sometimes expensive, so we prefer local if hit rate > X. what threshold do you suggest?
[05:15] Priya: it's workload dependent. for low-cost tokens you might pick any hit. we typically recommend tiered decision: prefer local when local_cache_hit_rate > 18% and predicted tail latency < 110ms; otherwise route to hosted for cheaper per-token cost but maybe higher egress. we can tune thresholds in the routing policy.
[05:33] Daniel: how do you predict hit-rate? is that a moving average?
[05:36] Priya: yes, we keep sliding windows and also per-route histograms. we use an exponential moving average with decay matched to request patterns — you can set the window to 5m, 1h, etc.
[05:46] [05:46] Rina: are there built-in metrics to surface prefix entropy and key density? we need to know if we should change normalization rules.
[05:54] Priya: console exposes prefix key cardinality, top-k hotset, and per-prefix hit rates. we'll share a sample dashboard.
[06:00] Marco: what about audit/logging for compliance? if a shared caching decision returns a response, we need an audit trail that shows the source and tenant decision.
[06:08] Priya: each cached response includes trace metadata: cache_id, originating_tenant, model_fingerprint, quant_profile, and a signed timestamp. for private deployments we can write these to your audit logs (and push to your SIEM).
[06:19] Evan: question from the architecture perspective — eviction. what's your current policy and how should you treat hot ephemeral prompts?
[06:26] Daniel: we currently use a ttl of 24 hours and LRU across the whole cluster. but we see big churn when new campaigns roll out.
[06:33] Priya: you might want adaptive TTLs: hotset entries get extended, whereas single-use prompts have short TTL. also tiered storage: very hot entries in memory, warm entries on nvme-backed cache nodes. and you can have tenant-weighted eviction to prevent noisy tenants from evicting others.
[06:51] Rina: tenant-weighted eviction sounds interesting — we have multi-tenant SLAs and want fairness controls. how's that configured?
[06:58] Priya: config is a per-tenant eviction weight. by default equal. you can set priority buckets; e.g., enterprise tenants get higher weight so their entries persist longer. it's enforced at cache partition or vbucket level to avoid cross-tenant imbalance.
[07:12] Daniel: do you partition by tenant hash? or by consistent hashing across nodes?
[07:16] Priya: consistent hashing across nodes with tenant-aware virtual nodes. that helps you reshard with lower movement. and for very large tenants you can pin a dedicated shard.
[07:25] Marco: how do you handle tenant migrations and key rotation? we rotate tenant ids for security every quarter.
[07:31] Priya: key rotation is supported — cache keys include a rotation epoch. when you rotate, prior keys become invalidated, but we support a migration window where both epochs are accepted. you'll see a brief cold period while hot keys rebuild.
[07:42] Evan: moving to safety — cache poisoning concerns, especially from public-facing tenants or abuse. how do you detect and mitigate?
[07:51] Priya: multi-prong: write-rate throttles, anomaly detection on output distribution (sudden shift in token probabilities), and a trust score per tenant. low-trust writes require manual validation or quarantine. we also sample cache writes for human review on sensitive classes.
[08:06] Daniel: ok and how about deterministic responses — if two tenants share an intent but one expects a branded wording, could a shared hit return wrong branding?
[08:14] Priya: that's why we include templating metadata and post-filters. shared hits return canonical content plus placeholders; the platform applies tenant-specific templating during response assembly. if templates differ, the system detects mismatch and aborts reuse.
[08:28] Rina: network question — when routing from on-prem to hosted, can you do secure peering? we need private connectivity without public egress.
[08:35] Priya: yes, for Private deployments we support VPC peering and private link. for on-prem we recommend VPN or direct interconnect; we support mutual TLS and customer-managed KMS for encryption of cache at rest.
[08:47] Marco: any limitations for air-gapped environments?
[08:50] Priya: in air-gapped mode, you can run the entire stack locally — but you lose hosted fallback. you can still use prefix caching and all routing decisions locally. we'll provide a packaged deployment that includes the cache service and control plane connectors for offline ops.
[09:02] Evan: let's talk bench specifics so we can size cache and set thresholds. Priya, can you list the data you'll need?
[09:08] Priya: sample logs with prompt text (or redacted versions), per-tenant traffic split, distribution of sequence lengths, and expected SLOs for p50/p95/p99 latency. also a list of tenants that require siloing.
[09:20] Daniel: we'll redact PII and provide synthetic mapping, we can get that to you by Sep 3.
[09:25] [09:25] Marco: for the benchmark, can we include quantization compatibility checks? like serve same prompt across bf16 and int8 and compare outputs.
[09:33] Priya: yes we'll include a compatibility sweep. we'll compute token-level and semantic similarity and flag regressions.
[09:39] Asha: batching - we want to reduce per-token cost but are worried about tail latency. how aggressive is Redwood's continuous batching?
[09:47] Priya: runtime uses adaptive batching that considers seq-len and latency budget. for interactive SLOs we limit max batch size and do prefix caching pre-checks to short-circuit. you can set latency targets and batching will auto-adjust. there's also prioritized small-batch lanes for low-latency traffic.
[10:06] Daniel: and autoscaling — if cache hit rate drops, we might see increased load to the model. how do you provision?
[10:11] Priya: autoscaling policies can be tied to miss-rate; e.g., if miss-rate exceeds 30% for 3 minutes, bring up additional model workers. you can also configure burst capacity.
[10:21] Evan: there's a question on storage backends — do you support redis, rocksdb, or custom in-memory kv?
[10:27] Priya: platform uses a custom in-memory KV with optional NVMe-backed LRU for warm items. we provide connectors to redis for teams that require it for compliance, but the native runtime is optimized for token streaming and KV-cache semantics.
[10:39] Rina: what's the memory footprint per cache entry? approximate average?
[10:42] Priya: depends on stored decoding state; for prefix-level entries we store compressed logits/kv-fragments. average compressed entry ~1.8KB for short prefixes, warm entries 6-8KB for longer contexts. this lets you estimate cluster size.
[10:58] Marco: that's helpful. okay let's talk about policy enforcement on read — do you do server-side checks for data exfil patterns?
[11:04] Priya: yes, there are read-time filters and data classification hooks. you can block reuse of cached outputs that contain sensitive markers. we also support redact-on-read for certain classes.
[11:15] Daniel: I want to raise a corner case — sequential prompts that build on previous responses (long chat histories). how do you key on prefixes without breaking context?
[11:24] Priya: for chat, we maintain a session-scoped KV cache that indexes on compressed dialogue state (not just raw text). that means re-use works when the compressed state matches. for mutable sessions we prefer per-session cache with short TTL.
[11:36] Evan: time check — about 15 minutes left — let's hit the dangerous scenarios and wrap with next steps.
[11:43] Rina: threat model: an attacker intentionally crafts prompts to poison the hotset to produce harmful responses. how do you mitigate?
[11:51] Priya: defenses include write throttles, trust tiers, and validation via a canary model. writes from new/untrusted tenants go to a quarantine area; only after a stability window are they promoted. we also run diff detectors comparing recent outputs to baseline semantics.
[12:07] Marco: legal asked about retention and log purging — can we set different retention per tenant?
[12:12] Priya: yes retention is per-tenant, and in private deployments you can configure physical deletion policies and KMS key lifecycle aligned with compliance needs.
[12:22] Daniel: last question — licensing and pricing implications of heavy cold-miss traffic to hosted models?
[12:28] Evan: price model depends on tokens served and reserved capacity. we can simulate cost curves given your hit rates and traffic profile. that's part of the benchmark deliverable.
[12:37] Asha: great.
[12:39] Evan: recap of next steps: we'll send the prefix key best-practices doc, security artifacts, and proposed benchmark run dates. Priya will own the bench config and Liam will assist on deployment runbooks. Luminex to share redacted logs and tenant list.
[12:56] Marco: sounds good, thanks everyone.
[12:59] Daniel: thanks — appreciate the pragmatic options.
[13:02] Priya: thanks all. we'll follow up with a calendar invite for the benchmark window.
